note: The known accessibility violations.
The browser scan is the only layer that can compute CONTRAST, because jsdom has no
layout: no boxes, no painted values, no cascade. So the contrast rule is disabled in
the unit layer and enabled here, in a real browser, with the stylesheet applied.
And the scan found real violations, which is what a scan is for. So they are written
down here rather than in a comment: a violation that is not recorded is a violation
nobody is going to fix, because the next person to run the gate sees a red and
assumes the gate is wrong.
The rule about an entry is the same as the rule about a refusal anywhere else in this
repository: the scan must find EXACTLY these violations and no others, and an entry
that no longer matches anything is a FAILURE, because a record that has gone stale is
an exemption nobody will ever revisit. A violation that gets FIXED is removed from
this file in the same commit that fixes it.
The key is the element's id, then its accessible name, then its text -- and NOT axe's
own target, which is a CSS selector built from class names. A record keyed on class
names has to be rewritten every time a style is refactored, and a record nobody keeps
is a record that absorbs whatever it is given.
Each entry says what closing it takes. That field is not optional: a violation with no
reason is a hole with a bookmark in it.
THE HONEST LIMIT. An axe scan is NOT accessibility. It catches the machine-detectable
minority -- roughly a third of WCAG issues. Meaningful reading order, alt-text
quality, error announcement and keyboard flow need a human with a screen reader, and
that human has not been in this repository yet. This file is a machine scan against
a known set, and `docs/status.md` says so in the same words.
2026-10-28: the four recorded violations were closed in one commit -- the top bar's
dimmed clock and service-principal text were lifted off the opacity token and onto
`--ink-2/--ink-3` which hold 4.5:1 on the panel ground, the search button's
accessible name was matched to its visible label by hiding the `Cmd-K` hint from
the accessibility tree, and the upload page's file input gained a real label. The
violations list is empty because the scan finds exactly the recorded violations and
no others.
